newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal leaders differ on EMU link with Spain.
newsitem.headline: Portugal leaders differ on EMU link with Spain.

text.p: Prime Minister Antonio Guterres and his long-serving predecessor Anibal Cavaco Silva agreed on Monday that Portugal should enter monetary union in the first group but differed over whether it could happen without Spain.

Opening a one-day conference on Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), Guterres reaffirmed his government's determination to be in the first wave of European Union countries wedding their economies in a single currency.

He said that Portugal was better-placed than other southern European countries because it had begun the process of adjusting its economy to the rigours of the planned Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) earlier than Spain or Italy.
"We are starting out from a more comfortable position than other countries in the Mediterranean basin," he said.
Portugal was determined to claim its place in the elite group regardless of what happened to neighbouring Spain, Guterres said, reaffirming what has long been the government line.

"Portugal can and should (enter the single currency) and her strategy must be one of autonomy with regard to geographical, political or other ties," he told the conference, organised by the Banco Portugues do Atlantico.
Portugal has performed slightly better than Spain on the budget deficit, one of the key EMU entry qualifications, but Spain comes closer to meeting limits on state debt.

Cavaco Silva, making one of his first appearances in a public forum since being defeated in a presidential election last January, said that it would be unrealistic to think of Portugal going in without Spain.

Cavaco Silva, who as Social Democrat prime minister took Portugal into the then European Community in 1986, said that it would be politically impossible for the European Union to choose one Iberian country without the other when a decision is taken on membership in the spring of 1998.
"On the contrary, Portugal's chances (of entering) would be greater if Spain were also considered elegible," he said.
Cavaco Silva said that the economic policies adopted by Portugal in the last few years had put the country on course to meet the EMU entry tests.
He said that the Portuguese escudo had been stable for the past three years since the last great crisis within the European Monetary System (EMS) and local interest rates had declined sharply.
"Portugal can do it, but it is going to depend on the implementation of the 1997 budget plan," he said.
Cavaco Silva refused at a news conference to comment on specific measures contained in the budget plan which the government has just sent to parliament.

The government's budget programme calls for the budget deficit to be cut to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), just under the EMU ceiling of three percent. The deficit is expected to be some four percent in 1996.
